back: A system whose correctness depends on the logical result AND the time at which it is produced.
Embedded: a dedicated function inside a larger system, not necessarily time bound. Real-time: timing constraints define correctness.
Hard: a miss is failure. Firm: a late result is useless and discarded. Soft: quality degrades; average response matters.
Periodic: fixed period, time driven. Aperiodic: irregular, event driven. Sporadic: irregular with a minimum inter-arrival time.
Delay, deadline and duration, each either a performance (system) or behavioural (environment) constraint.
A state that causes no damage when the system fails. Safety-critical systems have none, so they need very high reliability.
Error avoidance; error detection and removal; fault tolerance; built-in self-test.
Triple modular redundancy: three modules and a majority voter mask one faulty module.
N-version programming; recovery blocks; checkpointing and rollback.
Software failures are correlated (same design faults); redundancy costs time, so it only fits large deadlines.

Latency: the delay from input to response. Jitter: the variation in that timing.
An OS that gives logically correct results within deadlines: pre-emptive priority scheduling, bounded latency, small kernel.

Per-task record: ID, priority, state, saved context, stack, timing, resources.
Top half: short urgent ISR. Bottom half (DSR): deferred non-urgent processing in a task.
Clock driven: timer interrupts. Event driven: events. Hybrid: both.
